blocks.x: What was the man's name again that made that record?

I thought about the name of John Thompson. I wish I could think of the name of it. That was way back around 19... ...six or seven. I couldn't think of the name not to save my life, but the number. But it was a ragtime tune or a jazz tune you'd say? It was a ragtime number. Something like at those times, they called them numbers a one step. Dancers, we called them a one step.
And how old would you be when you first heard the record, do you say?
I was around about six, seven years old.
And your father had had the record for a number of years.

I'll tell you the truth. I don't know how long my dad had had that record. I used to hear him play it a lot. He used to play it a lot on Sundays when his band used to come down at a rehearsal. Mm-hmm. And they played that record a lot to learn it. And they learned to play it pretty good too. Yeah, that particular record they learned it pretty good.
But when you say that record was hot music, jazz music, just like they played here in 1920s? Was it on that style? No, no, no, no.
It wasn't on that style at all. What style was it? It was on, just a ragtime style playing music.
Did they sound like they were reading?
Well, I don't know.
You don't remember the record that clearly, I know.
No, and at that time if there's reading, I didn't know anyway. Yeah. I was too young to know, just reading or just playing by air. I'd like to have it now. Just for memories, you know.
Mm-hmm. Maybe we'll run across it. Was it a cylinder or a flat racket?
I always made something like this, you know, something like that.
A round cylinder? Yeah, it was a round. What's it called a cylinder? Yeah, a round racket. Yeah. It wasn't a flat one. It wasn't like this. It was a cup, they call them also.

Yeah, it was round. It wasn't a flat one like they make these days. It was round ones. But it was a good record because I think my daddy had it quite a while and we played it a lot. And when he wasn't there, we was playing it a lot. We had about 10 or 15 records round there. We'd, you know what I mean, just pick them up and play them any of them. Mm-hmm. And, but I think Thompson had about the best band at that time, so we just, just keep playing over and over and over. And just jumping, dancing, hollering, and go play it again. They had this, what do you call those things? A wind up song? Yeah, yeah. Like an Edison. Wind it up and they had big bells on it, sit out there. I forgot what they called, used to call them, phonographs or something like that.
Yeah, that's huh. Grammophones is another name, do I get. Orthophonics they used to call them.
U stuff I forgot what they called, used to call them, phonographs or something like that.
Grammophones is another name, do I get? Orthophonics they used to call them.
Used to call them orthophonics.
Now how did you know the date the record was made?
No, I didn't write it down, but we used to argue about it so much.
Oh, I see.
My cousin and I, he'd want to say it was made in one year and I'd say it was made in another, we'd run back home and get the record. Look on it.
And it had it written on the record?
Yeah, it was on there. And it had the date on there.
Well, we'll try to find it.
I don't know where you're going to find it.
Oh, I know a guy who collects those things, right? Oh, yeah. The clarinet player? Yeah, yeah.
He collects those old records like that.
Oh, yeah.
Well, he might find it then. Matter of fact, I think those old men broke up a lot of old records he had about five, six years ago. Mm. Just threw them out of the yard, broke them all up.
That's terrible. Mm-hmm. Shouldn't do that when things are worth money.

Well, I didn't know those wastes and things. No, he didn't know those wastes. He just got tired of laying around there in the way. He just threw them out of the yard and broke them up. Had about 12, 15 of them he threw out there. Trash. After he joined church, he don't worry what does no more. So, sit down and look at television. That's his biggest, I don't know, sit down after he come awake and look at television and sleep.
Is he still alive?
Oh, yeah, sure.
Where does he live?
In Paschristian, Mississippi. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.
You got his address? I might look him up when I go over there.
Yeah. No. I got it, but it's in the room in there.

Okay, well, we'll get it later. Yeah. Because there's several fellas I want to look up over there, you know. Oh, yeah. Probably still several bands going, you know. I was planning to make a trip over there to see Isaiah Morgan, but he came here.
Oh, yeah, well, he was in Biloxi, though.
Yeah.
Mm-hmm. Yeah, he's here.
What's your father's full name? You told me once, John Handy Sr. Yeah. That's his name, yeah. Well, we wouldn't have any trouble finding him if we got over there anyway.
Oh, no, you just ask anybody for him. A little children up to the old one. They'll tell you who he is. If they can find him, if he be working in a day.
What's his age now? Is he?
What's your little? The little man's around 70. 78. Yeah, he's around that age.
He's 20 when you were born. Yeah, just about 20. Yeah. Yeah. Mm-hmm.
My mother's 78, too. You know my mother, though?
Oh, yeah?
Yeah. She's 78. My daddy's 78. She's pretty sick now, though.
Oh, your mother? Mm-hmm. A lot of people have been sick lately.
Yeah, they've been sitting up with her for the last couple of weeks. My sister's got a bad heart. Bad touch on her. Heart failure or something.
You know, Eddie Pearson is sick. Supposed to be in charity last time.

Yeah, well, he's still in there. Yeah, that's true. Mm-hmm. Matter of fact, I played over there Friday, Friday evening at a charity. Mm-hmm. And, uh, but I didn't get a chance to go up there and see him, because I had to, I had to work out at the country club Friday night, and when we left there, it was late. So I had to rush home and get me something to eat, and then change clothes, and go pick up my brother, and rush out to the country club.
I wanted to ask you, who were some of the best clarinet players in New Orleans when you first came here?
Oh, when I first came here, I liked it, uh, Joe Watson with Sam Morgan.
Mm-hmm.

I liked it, him for clarinet. Mm-hmm. And then I had another fellow, I liked it pretty good, played with Rene, called him Zib. Oh, yeah. Yeah, he was a nice clarinet player. Mm-hmm. And then I had this fellow, Blind Freddy. Mm-hmm. Wonderful. He could play about as much clarinet with one piece of it, he's the average guy to play with the whole horn. Mm-hmm. And he was a wonderful harmonica player, too. I think he still plays, I don't know.
I don't know.

He maybe do, but I haven't seen him play in a long time. Matter of fact, I haven't heard him play anything in a long time. I run across him every night, and then, yeah, he passes by my house. Mm-hmm. And then I had this fellow, T.O. used to play a lot of clarinet, too, with P. Ron. But he was mostly a reading man, to sit out and play that music.
Well, how did he do if he got in some Barrel House place and had to cut loose? Suppose he...
He never was there.
He would never sit in with a band? No.

I never was going to go, no. Never would get him sit in with a body. Played strictly with P. Ron. And after he finished that, that's it all. Matter of fact, he'd go home, he would never come around us, no way. Mm-hmm. No, unless he was passing there, and the rest of the band stopped there for, listened for a while. He might stand up there and listen, but he soon disappeared, he'd go.
Well, what about those guys like him, the reading guys? Did they come around much and listen to the real, uh, rag-down jazz musicians?

Well, they used to come around occasionally. They didn't come too often. They was kind of a set of fellows that, uh, they didn't think he was doing right. That's what they, that was their idea, by the way.
They thought, they thought music was the only way.

Only way, yeah. Mm-hmm. So they didn't care too much about our style of playing, and they didn't come around too much. Now, P. Ron used to be around often, him. P. Ron used to come often, you couldn't keep Steve Lewis away from that, him. Steve was just an addict to music.
What kind of guy was Steve Lewis? Steve Lewis? Mm-hmm.
Oh, Steve Lewis is a wonderful piano player. Likes to crack a lot of jokes, and he sing a lot of songs with a lot of smutty things to it.
I don't know. Did you ever know Papa D. Dot Dot? No, I don't think. You ever know Papa D. Dot Dot? No, I don't think. You ever know Papa D. Dot Dot? No, I don't think.
You ever know Papa D. Dot Dot? No, I don't think.

I don't think I know. He was one of Steve's buddies. He was always getting in trouble, you know, and Steve would get him out of jail. Oh, yeah? No, I don't know him. Uh, what would these songs be about that Steve Lewis would sing?

Anything come in his mind. Yeah, anything come in his mind, he'd say it. Yeah, he didn't care what he said, the way he said it, anything come in his mind, he'd say stuff I know he was playing there on the Island Charter. Man you couldn't get in the place. From the time he get there and the time he leave. He get there around. He do that eight. He get there around ten, eleven. Anytime. But the people still be there waiting for him when he come in. Man he walk back there and the people give him a big glass of whiskey with the served beer. That's what they give him whiskey. He take him a big drink of there and sit on the piano. Man he started singing back there. And there's no way in the world for you to get back there to him. All the people around him. Just giving him money. Making him sing. Giving him money. Making him sing. And get him drunk. And then they used to take him from there. He used to leave there around three or four o'clock in the morning. They take him from there. They take him to the Roosevelt Hotel. Somewhere up in there. And have him sing up there until nine, ten o'clock the next day. He made a lot of money. Then he was a, you know, thing. Then he was a, he was a regular guy. Fine, fine guy, Steve was. That's the only fault P. Roy had of him drinking so much. Never messed up. He'd go ahead and play but he just, he likes to drink. And then P. Roy didn't like that. Did you work much with P. Roy? No. No, I didn't do much playing with P. Roy because P. Roy had a lot of hard music and I couldn't cut it. That's good. He wouldn't run an affair with your playing or something. Yeah, well I didn't, uh, he kept a lot of stock. I don't even. He kept a lot of arrangements for his band. And, uh, I used to do a lot of rehearsals. And, uh, for you to just go sit in there, you had to be pretty good. Excuse me, go ahead. Unless he was playing Dinah or High Society or something like that.
Well, you could get in there like that. But, uh, I knew he'd play them. He was Edward Quest as far.
And other of his music he was, wrote there to play strictly about his music. And he was playing out there at Transcenius and, uh, and, uh, he was playing for the better class of...

and they didn't go for too much of that, you know, rock music, so all this stuff was smooth and soft, things like that. Then he had you playing it note for note and crescendos and different things. That's the way you wanted it played, and that's the way you had to play it for him. So for you to go sit in his band, you understand what I mean. You got to be a pretty polished musician to go sit in his band.
Well, who liked jazz music in those days, say in the 20s when you were here?
Well, practically everybody around here. You wanted to like that because...
Did you say P-Ron would play for a special class of people though, huh?

Yeah, he played for the better class of people, see. He played for the doctors and the lawyers and people up here on St. Charles Street, people back in the place and all that kind of people, the higher class of people, see. And they liked that sweet music and slow and waltzes a lot of things, you know, something like that. Well, the average band around here didn't play that, see. Like John Robeshoe and P-Ron. And they had another fellow here called Peter Bocard and his bunch. Now they played all that kind of music. But we went on down and got on the gutter. Bounced them around a little bit. Well, that's what they liked. We used to go down to the old Corporate's Hall down there and start playing down there around 8 o'clock. And he'd do it at the night and play until 2 or 4 o'clock the next morning. Corporate's, the economy. And then, uh, uh, uh, Sanderson, yeah, he was there then. And they had another hall up there on Howard Avenue. It's just back in the yard. I forgets the name of that. I know we come down here from Baton Rouge to play a contest against, uh, Celestan over there. And I believe that was the first time a lot of those guys heard me play clarinet was in Celestan's band at that time. Who won the contest? Tup. Tup. Tup Johnson won it.
He had a good band. I had a good band.

Well, that's just like anything else. I don't know. They say Tup's won it, but I don't know. You take, uh, maybe that's because that was the first time they heard Tup's band. Everybody liked it. That didn't prove that they had a better band than Celestan. But, uh, first time hearing something, it sounds good to you. I imagine if they stayed around there three, four weeks or a month or so, they would have forgot about him. See you. But that particular one night stand, they go with people. Of course, I was with me at a good band though.
Did they have one guy who would be acclaimed, the best clarinet player in town, be chosen at any time?
Over here?
Yeah. He's an ambition. He was considered by who to be the best? Everybody. Everybody. Musicians? Listeners? Everybody.
Everybody considered him to be the best.

And then after he left? Then I come in the picture. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. And, uh, how long did you stay, well, what did they call the guy who was the best clarinet player? Did he have a special name? No, nothing. Like, a clarinet king or anything like that?
No, just called him by his regular name.
Yeah. I thought maybe they gave him a title. No. Like, kid or king or something, you know?
No. They called him by his regular name. Yeah. Mm-hmm.
And so, uh, you came in the picture after Bechet.
After Bechet left here.
And then you put the clarinet down, huh?
I put it down for Alto Satchipa. Mm-hmm.
And who took up on clarinet after that? Who would you say? Well, I'm not. Oh, but any, was anybody on clarinet?
Yeah, George Lewis. You'd say he was the king?
Yeah, he was, he was about to next to me. He was George Lewis. When did George Lewis start coming in the public eye, would you say?

Well, George started coming in the eye of the public around, I'd say around 22. Mm-hmm. In 1922. Because we was playing at, uh, at, uh, Humming Booth, at, uh, Elite. And when we'd get through there, I had a place back, Iberville Street, that, Iberville and Mariette called, uh, the Boothwa. Uh, all the musicians used to go back there when they get off on wake. All of them used to go back there to jam. Jam that is six, seven o'clock the next morning. Well, George was playing a lot of clarinet then. So I'd say he was about to next around here.
And was his style similar to his today or different?
No, just about the same as it is today.
Mm-hmm. Same style.

Now I could tell him anywhere he had. Same style he played on. And then, uh, Willie Humphrey stepped in the picture then. Because he's a little clarinet player than either one of us. But he stepped in the picture after, uh, George began to travel.
And then Willie Humphrey come out.

But they got, uh, some clarinet players around here that you know are here so often. Great. You take the president of our local, Louis Contrero. Mm-hmm. Great clarinet player. Great. You know, he'll, you know, hear much of him. But he's a great clarinet player. I only got another boy around here that plays a lot of clarinet. Uh, I can't think of his name. I can't think of his name now. He's Harold DeVos Jones' brother-in-law. I can't think of his name. Right now. He plays a lot of clarinet too.
Have you ever heard of Manuel Krustow or whatever his name? That's who I'm talking about, Manuel.
Manuel Krustow. He plays a lot of clarinet too. He's in my mind reader.
Yeah, he must be. He must be because that's who I was talking about, Manuel. Does he work at all now? What does he do?
He just spots him up. I don't know what Manuel's doing now. I know he's working in a day someplace. He's a pastor or a carpenter or something like that.
I don't think he's doing much playing at night time. Manuel's a fellow that, uh, he's a pastor or a carpenter or something like that.

I don't think he's doing much playing at night time. Manuel's a fellow that, uh, he's a nice musician and he plays a lot. He knows a lot of instruments. I mean he knows a lot of trumpet, he knows a lot of sax, and he knows a lot of clarinet. Well, he's a swell guy as long as he's not drinking. But if he get to drinking, he'll have to walk off to the Roosevelt Hotel and leave you there. On and all, he'll leave it. He get to drinking. That mind hit him. He jumped right about that chair and walked straight on out there. And you don't see him no more until the next day or two, three weeks or something like that. You see, that's the kind of type of fellow he is. What does he drink?
He can drink anything you drink, but he just gets to rambling mind or something.

I don't know. A lot of people are scared of him. He's allowed to hire him and he's allowed to jump up and leave any minute if he gets to drinking. Not long as he's not drinking, he loves to work. He loves to play them instruments. All of them. But that's the trouble. You have to stop him from playing sometimes when he's not drinking. He's allowed to. He's allowed to leave. He's allowed to leave. He's allowed to leave. People get scared of him like that. See. That's the same way with Sonny Johnson. He's scared of him. He's allowed to. Matter of fact, he's more apt to not to come. He's to leave when he gets to. He's a great outdoor player. He's scared of him. He's allowed to. He's allowed to be there. He's allowed to be there. He된 stuff One of the greatest alto players in the city today. He's a great alto player. He's scared of him. He's liable to him. Matter of fact, he's more apt to not to come. He is to leave when he gets there. If you ever get him there, he won't leave, but trouble is to getting him there. That's some trouble. But he's a great man. And he can play a lot of clarinet too. You never heard him play clarinet?
Never.
Man, he's a great clarinet player.
Never heard him. You never heard him play? Never found him. Huh? He always plays with somebody where I'm not there, it seems like. You know? It's funny.

And he's a very quiet guy. He don't say nothing to nobody. He said that. And I bet he'd sit up there and play all night and wouldn't say three words. Never say nothing. Unless you ask him something. You ask him something. He'd give you that flat answer then. That's all. No more talk. He's a peculiar guy. He won't talk. He talk too much when he get to drinking. But there is only me drinking. He don't drink that much. At least he didn't used to drink. I haven't seen him now in about eight, nine months. He's a great clarinet player. Matter of fact, he's a great musician. Because he'd been, he was teaching over there at Will Irons. Taught there for good. Why? You didn't see him there? Well, never. Well, never. What happened to you in Louisiana? Well, I've never seen him. I've never seen him. I've never seen him. I've never seen him. At least he didn't used to drink. I haven't seen him now in about eight, nine months. But he's a great, he's a great, great alto player. He's a great clarinet player. Matter of fact, he's a great musician. Cause he'd been, he was teaching over there at Will Irons. Taught there for good. Why? You didn't see him there? Well, never. Well, what happened to your Louisiana Shakers? You were telling me about that band. Did they bust up or? Yeah, I left here and went to St. Louis. Oh yeah, we got up there. Yeah. And then what happened? You came back here from St. Louis. Oh yeah, we got up there. Yeah.
And then what happened? You came back here from St. Louis? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. You came back from St. Louis, I think you tell them.

No, I left St. Louis and I went to Springfield. I played out in Springfield for six, seven months out there. And I got sick. Matter of fact, I was sick when I went there. And I had to leave Springfield to come back in because I was about dying on my feet up there with my stomach. And I left and come back here. I went back to Pastor Christian and opened up maybe a little business and kept that up for about two, three years. My stomach fell. I started feeling better. I left there and came back over here. I left there and come back over here.
You had your own business then?
Yeah.
Mm-hmm.
I left there and come back over here and started playing again. Did you ever play at home in Pastor Christian?
Oh, yeah. Yeah.
I played there a lot of times.
While you had your business, I mean. Did you just?
Yeah, yeah. I played once or twice.
I couldn't do more playing though because my stomach was bad. Mm-hmm. Played every now and then. I'd play a job maybe.
What happens when your stomach's bad? Do you play? What does it do? It's not bad anymore. Mm-hmm. But I mean it gives you a bad tone or somethin'? No. It stuff
What happens when your stomach's bad? Do you plan? What does it do?
It's not bad anymore.
But I mean it gives you a bad tone or something?

No, it stops you from playing and pains yourself. Yeah, it's a pain. I remember when I was playing to LeVito at Lee Collins and then, I had a quarter of whiskey on this side and a quarter of cooking soda water on this side. I'd be standing up taking the soda on my horn and boom. When the pains hit you and double you up, you drink that soda water quick. You sit down there for about three or four minutes and it'll pass away. But when it hits you like that, you got to do something. I suffered my stomach since 19... 1913. I remember when the first pain hit me on a Friday evening, coming from Wake.
Since 19 when?
You were 13 years old?

I had pneumonia, typhoromalary, fever, heart liver. Ah, something else. I had all that at once when I was around 12 years old. Yeah. I saw a doctor by the name of Dr. Woodson. Killed me of it, but he told him I'd always have something. I always suffer with something. And that's where they left me with a bad stomach.
Well, when you stopped your business in Pastor Christian and came over here, who did you play with?
All different fellas. I never had no particular one to play with. Just afternoon I was in town. He called me up, asked me to work and I'd accept the job.
Never worked with Ken Howland? Oh yeah, Howland and I had a band together.
When was that?
Oh that was back in the 30s.
Yeah we had a band together.
As a matter of fact I tried to get Howard to keep the band going when I went to St. Louis. He said he was but business run out on him I suppose. Because I was getting most of the work.
Now who took your place in that band when you left for St. Louis?

I don't know. That's something I never did find out. Because I don't think it stayed together much longer after I left. Because I was doing all the booking and that's what was keeping the band together. See some work if you didn't have no work you couldn't keep the band together. So I was doing all the booking. When I left they had to stop the booking see. So I didn't do much playing. Of course Howard had a few jobs. And they didn't want a big band because I had 10, 11, or 12 pieces in my band. At that time they just wanted to. Howard was getting a lot of six piece jobs. You know how long that's going to keep the big band together. Take the six out of the playing. First opportunity they got to join another band they just left.
So that was the end of the Louisiana Shakers. So when did you come back to town from Paschristown? What year was that?
Oh I don't know exactly when I left Paschristown and come back here.
Was that during World War II or after? No no. After? Before? World War II I was in Paschristown then.
And I don't remember what year I left there and come back over here. But I was there in World War II alone.
I'm trying to remember some of the different people I heard you with you know. Since 1949 like Howard, Annie Williams some.
Yeah.
